Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Tamworth District Court
Marius St & Fitzroy Street,
Tamworth NSW 2340
Wednesday, 18 September 2024 at 9.32am
(Day 51)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hernan Pintos-Lopez for
NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR GLOVER: Commissioner, this morning we have Dr Ramsey
Awad, whose presentation I mentioned briefly in opening
yesterday.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR GLOVER: He is joining us by AVL and he is on the
screen now.
THE COMMISSIONER: Dr Awad, good morning.
THE WITNESS: Good morning, Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: You can obviously hear me. Would you
like to give your evidence by way of oath or affirmation?
THE WITNESS: Affirmation, please, Commissioner.
<RAMSEY AWAD, AFFIRMED [9.32 am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR FULLER
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR GLOVER: Q. Dr Awad, in a moment you may be able to
see me, but can you at least for the present time hear me
okay?
A. I can. Thank you.
Q. Right. If at any stage the connection breaks up and
you can't hear me or need something repeated, just let me
know, all right?
A. Thank you.
Q. Can you tell us your full name, please?
A. So it's Ramsey Awad, A-W-A-D.
Q. And you are the executive director infrastructure,
planning and sustainability in the Hunter New England Local
Health District?
A. That is correct.
Q. What does that mean, on a day-to-day basis?
A. It means lots of things. There are several parts to
my portfolio. One is clinical planning. So that unit

works on what are the clinical needs for our
Hunter-New England communities now and into the future for
the next 20 years, so working out what services we want and
where. The other part of the portfolio is infrastructure
delivery. So we have - over these last five years, we have
about $2.5 billion worth of infrastructure that is
underway, a lot of it in regional New England. A lot of
new hospitals going up. Engineering and maintenance, so
maintaining all our existing facilities and hospitals, old
and new, and sustainability is also a large part of my
portfolio and there are some other bits and pieces which we
don't need to get into, but it is a broad portfolio within
the district.
Q. Thank you. Before we get into the reason why we have
brought you along today, can you just tell us a little bit
about your professional background prior to landing in this
role?
A. Absolutely. So my education is in - I have degrees in
architecture and construction project management and PhDs
in - a PhD in health and infrastructure and change
management. I have worked for NSW Health at the ministry
level, rolling out statewide change management performance
improvement programs for NSW Health. I have worked in the
construction industry delivering high risk New South Wales
Government projects for the Olympics, the Circular Quay
redevelopment, the Walsh Bay redevelopment, and I have
spent the majority of my career working in health and
either on the change operational side of things or
delivering major infrastructure projects. And I've also
worked for Ernst & Young as their executive director for
government advisory in the particular focus of government
and health.
Q. Thank you.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. How did health and infrastructure
find its way under the one PhD thesis, what was it on?
A. Well, it married - we looked at every emergency
department that was built on the east coast of Australia
for the last 25 years, and the question was: does new
infrastructure actually make a difference in terms of the
metrics we use to measure the performance of an emergency
department in terms of triage times and throughput and
morbidity? Because everyone thinks you get the new
emergency department and everything gets better. The
answer is in 70 per cent of every emergency department

we've built in this country, at least the majority of the
country, there is no improvement in performance.
Q. Was that surprising to find that out?
A. It's surprising for other people to hear that. It
wasn't surprising for me, having worked in the industry for
a while. 40 per cent actually get worse when they get a
new emergency department. 30 per cent --
Q. Just stop there. Stop there. Why do 40 per cent get
worse?
A. Because what they do is they create more space and
they redesign the physical space and theoretically the
flows, but in parallel they don't redesign all the business
processes, the clinical processes that are required. So
one of the things that I've introduced in my current role
is when we do a new infrastructure project, I have a whole
team that focuses on the operational change management that
needs to occur, working with those frontline clinical staff
to say, "Hey, you got a new space but how are you going to
be working in a new and a different way that improves your
effectiveness and efficiency in that?" So you have to do
things in parallel.
Q. Sorry, I interrupted you. You had mentioned that
40 per cent don't improve, but you were about to say
30 per cent, and then I interrupted you.
A. Thank you. No, that's okay, Commissioner.
30 per cent don't change at all; they continue to maintain
their current performance. And there's 30 per cent that do
improve. And the ones that do improve - and this links
back to when I worked at the ministry, which was developing
clinical redesign methodology, which occurred back - we
started a process here at the John Hunter Hospital where we
redesigned our systems and processes around patients - this
is back in 2002 - and it has spawned, I guess, this
methodology which exists all through Australia now, which
is to, in tandem to delivering infrastructure or even if
you're not delivering infrastructure, redesigning the
systems and processes in a very structured way that brings
people along with you, but also looks at the hard data, so
you make the right decisions, because often in change
management, you have two extremes.
The consultants will come in and provide their advice
and a report and the staff, you know, tell them to get
lost, that we're not interested, or you allow the staff to

form committees and those committees often meet for a few
years and it's often the person with the loudest voice gets
what they want or nothing gets delivered at all. So this
methodology that we delivered and developed 20 years ago
combines those two elements to deliver real fundamental
change, and one of the pieces of work I did for the
Ministry of Health when I worked there was to set up a
school. It is called the Centre for Healthcare Redesign,
it is part of NSW Health, it has been running now for,
I think, 15 years, and it gives our frontline managers,
those change management skills and clinical redesign skills
which are core, I think, to evolving the health service.
Q. Because I have opened this up, I better make sure
I understand it fully. Of the 40 per cent that you say -
so 40/30/30 are the percentages?
A. Correct.
Q. Of the 40 per cent that don't improve, having had a
new ED, what are you measuring in terms of improvement?
I imagine one would be wait times probably, but I don't
know. You tell me what you were measuring for that?
A. You're spot-on, Commissioner. It is the triage time,
so all the different categories 1 through 5. We measured
morbidity as well. We measured return patients that were
discharged, then returned to the ED. The only metric that
went up was, I guess, staff and patients satisfaction in
terms of the environment, that it felt nicer, it was
cleaner, it was - and everything was new. That metric
went --
Q. Not as cramped?
A. Not as cramped. So that was an improvement. But in
terms of how we measure how well an emergency department is
performing, it didn't improve in a lot of the cases.
THE COMMISSIONER: Okay. We might have to make a call for
your PhD thesis and get it tendered.
MR GLOVER: I was about to do the same thing.
Q. Dr Awad, one of the projects that you are currently
working on and implementing within the LHD is a
sustainability project, correct?
A. Correct.
Q. And we had the benefit of a presentation of yours on

Monday, and what I'm going to do is invite you to tell us a
little bit about that project by reference to some slides
that you have helpfully provided us. But before we get to
the slides, can you just tell us what was the catalyst for
this project?
A. It was our board chair, former board chair, Lyn
Fragar. She was interested in sustainability and thought
that we should be doing something as a district and as an
organisation. She spoke to our then chief executive
Michael Di Rienzo and asked him to put some energy into it
and find someone to look at it. I had just started in this
particular role, sustainability wasn't part of my job
description, and, you know, there was a knock at my door
and said, "Can you - there is a board meeting next week.
Can you put something together for sustainability?"
I presented next week, really the following week, one
slide which was that we would be carbon and waste neutral
by 2030 in this district, and the board were very excited,
I think the chief executive was a bit worried about what
I had committed us to, and then I outlined how we would do
that. And with my background in change management in large
organisations, I built a lot of our approach and strategy
around that. I am not an expert in sustainability, or
I wasn't when I started, but that was the catalyst of the
project and we just got on with it.
Q. I'll have the slides brought up on the screen,
Dr Awad. Can you see those slides? You are no doubt
familiar with them?
A. I am familiar but I can't see them, I'm sorry. Yes,
I can now.
Q. You can see them now?
A. Yes.
Q. All right. If we pass over the title page.
A. Please.
Q. And we acknowledge Country, as always. And then if we
go to the third page, "why is a green vision?"
A. Yes.
Q. You see that?
A. I can.
Q. Now, can you just talk us through the concepts that

are described in this slide?
A. Absolutely. So World Health Organisation, in their
research, have told us that 25 per cent of all human
disease and death now can be linked to environmental
factors, and with children that's higher, it's at
36 per cent. So that's globally known as a fact. We, at
the time - we're about to go into a drought season again -
New England, in particular, has been at the forefront of a
lot of those changes in terms of bushfires and drought.
And when you look at the emissions that healthcare, the
delivery of healthcare, generate in this country, they're
at 7 per cent, so that gives you some context on that. The
construction --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Can I just pause you there.
A. Of course.
Q. The 25 per cent figure is sourced from WHO?
A. Correct.
Q. I think it can be taken as well-known that Australia
and New South Wales is subject to climate change and
extreme climate events, such as floods and also drought,
and a lack of water security from time to time, and
certainly projected for the future. Is there a figure,
though, of that 25 per cent? Is there a figure for
Australia that you're aware of?
A. No, I'm not aware of a figure particularly for
Australia, Commissioner.
Q. And the 7 per cent of healthcare emissions, that is
sourced from where?
A. I can provide that source for you.
Q. You can take it on notice and tell us later, yes.
A. Absolutely.
Q. Thanks.
A. So the provision of healthcare, as you said, is
7 per cent. To give you some context, the construction
industry in Australia - and that includes roads, mining,
commercial, residential construction, per annum produces
about 15 per cent of our emissions. So we're about half of
that and when you put that into the context of how much
construction goes on in this country, you get a sense that
it is still a significant amount, and Health is, out of all
government agencies, is by far the largest contributor to

emissions. Just the sheer nature of our scale and the
amount of facilities that we own and the 24-hour nature of
our facilities.
So, we made a decision as an organisation that if we
are in the game and the role of healthcare that we needed
to play a very strong role in working towards reducing our
contribution to those environmental factors which are
causing human disease.
MR GLOVER: Q. Thank you. If we go to the next slide.
These are the three core principles of the vision; is that
right?
A. Correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. I think you told us that "waste
neutral" relates to landfill, correct?
A. That is correct, Commissioner. Would you like me to
elaborate on any of these, or?
MR GLOVER: Q. Yes, please.
A. Okay, sure. So the vision is to be carbon neutral,
which a lot of government and non-government organisations
are committing to by - in certain periods. We also want to
be waste neutral by 2030. We set ourselves a 10-year
window to achieve that. It is a very ambitious target and
I can foresee some hurdles in us achieving that moving
forward, unless there is some further support from policy
from government that's going to be required to achieve
that. But that's the target we've set.
Q. What sort of hurdles, firstly, do you envisage in
reaching that aim?
A. Just broadly, the biggest hurdle will be with regards
to green energy. By far the biggest contributor to carbon
emissions is the generation of electricity. That's
probably 80 to 90 per cent of it. We at the moment are
supplementing that through solar, but I will give you a
good example. The John Hunter Hospital, which is the
busiest trauma centre in New South Wales, the second
busiest in the country, it is a large hospital, does have
the largest solar panel installation in the world sitting
on top of its roof. It is about a kilometre long. All of
those solar panels only produce about 10 to 15 per cent of
the energy that actually John Hunter uses each year.
So although it is enormous and impressive, it is

nowhere near what is required to eliminate the coal-fired
energy that we utilise. So what's going to have to - and
we can buy green energy. That is, we have a statewide
government contract, I believe with Shell, for all our
energy supply. They do offer green energy. I can buy
green energy for John Hunter, but it will cost me a couple
of million dollars a year to do that and in a very tight
financial environment, it's not really feasible to do that.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. That final shift is going to rely
on government shifting the electricity market more towards
renewables than relying on coal?
A. Absolutely.
Q. Yes.
A. You are 100 per cent right. So we're looking at
on-ground solar, we are looking at other ways we can reduce
our energy consumption, but I know that I'm going to reach
a stage in the next couple of years that for us to reach
that zero target, I am going to need to buy green energy,
and it is a question of how much that costs in a couple of
years. And we have a real opportunity. See, John Hunter
hospital with the solar we currently have, if we were to
purchase green energy now, we could actually announce the
first carbon neutral hospital in this country. It's within
our grasp. It's really a financial hurdle which is
stopping us doing that at the moment.
Q. Do you know roughly how much more it would cost than
current costs if you did that?
A. About $2 million per annum.
Q. Just for John Hunter?
A. Just for John Hunter, correct.
MR GLOVER: Q. You mentioned requiring government
support. In addition to support to shift to green energy
more generally, is there anything else by way of support
you see as being needed to achieve the carbon neutral by
the 2030 goal?
A. Look, I think at a State level, greater coordination
is required. And the reason I say that is at the moment,
I think - well, I know that the secretary and the ministry
are very much on board with sustainability as an important
item of what we need to - important agenda item that we
need to focus on. What we can improve on, though, is
coordination. I - at the moment, I think within the

ministry there is probably six or seven groups that are
working on sustainability, which is great. The ability to
coordinate them, I think there are some real opportunities
there.
Then you have 15 LHDs, which are all focusing on
sustainability. Then you have got these other government,
New South Wales government, agencies and treasury and
others which have a sustainability agenda. You have got
the Federal Government that has a sustainability agenda,
and then you've got private sector university research
groups that are focusing on sustainability as well. It's
fantastic that everyone is playing in this space, but,
ultimately, I feel like you need - and the NHS has a
sustainability officer, but it needs to bring all these
people together. And the reason being that there is lots
of energy being put into those individual groups, but from
my perspective we need to do this work quickly, we need to
identify what are the high value items that we need to
pursue as a state government agency, as NSW Health, and
what do I define as high value? I think one is reducing
emissions and waste, but more important in the current
fiscal environment is reducing cost.
So if it was up to me, I would identify the top 10 or
20 major initiatives that we're going to pursue as an
organisation, align all those separate groups to those
initiatives, and get on with it and really make some gains.
And, importantly, if we ensure that those elements are
cost-based, then re-invest the money we save into frontline
clinical services, because that's where - that's our core
business at the end of the day.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. But just sticking with carbon and
being carbon neutral by 2030, that - I mean, that's
ambitious. I'm not suggesting it's bad ambition, it's good
ambition, but it is a fair way ahead of the New South Wales
government legislated targets to get to net zero by,
I think, 2050, with some interim targets on the way. So
you are just setting yourself a massive challenge there
beyond what is legislated.
A. I get bored easily, Commissioner.
Q. Oh, okay.
A. It's something to do.
Q. Well, better 2030 than 2080, I'm sure. So, yes.

A. Yes.
MR GLOVER: Q. And - sorry, Doctor?
A. No, that's okay. Just to finish that thought
regarding what else we could be doing, I think also one of
the things ministry has been helping with is allowing our
staff - this is a change management exercise as much as,
you know, reducing emissions; we want to win the hearts and
minds of people. They have introduced, you know, funding
for our clinical staff to develop sustainability
initiatives and ideas, which is great. I think what else
we could be doing to assist in that is knowledge
management, and, you know, taking those good ideas and
super-charging them and rolling them out across the whole
state very quickly is something, I think, is a real
opportunity for the ministry to be pursuing.
Q. What you are describing is greater coordination of
effort and then with the ability to scale up those
successful initiatives quickly across the board; is that
the idea?
A. Correct, and to prioritise the initiatives which are
going to help us achieve our goals, and the goal has to
include saving dollars for Health.
Q. And we'll come to it in due course, but some of the
initiatives that you have implemented in the district are
already seeing some financial benefits, aren't they?
A. Correct.
Q. You tell us a little about the goal to be waste
neutral by 2030? The Commissioner clarified with you
earlier that's about landfill, but tell us a little bit
more about that initiative and how it is going to be
achieved.
A. Absolutely. So when we started in 2020, 92 per cent
of our waste was going to landfill for Hunter New England
Health. We want it to be zero by 2030. That is by far the
hardest thing for us to achieve, for a number of reasons.
One is we have to deal with clinical waste, which has to be
dealt with in a particular sort of way in terms of its
disposal and requires some legislative changes and some
work with the EPA to maybe dispose of that clinical waste
in a different and new way. But if we just focus on
general waste, it is dependent on a number of factors. One
is, particularly as you move further away from major
centres like Sydney and Newcastle, you are reliant on the

councils having the ability to manage different types of
waste, so organic waste, plastic waste, et cetera. They
need the infrastructure and the systems to take that waste
and do something which is more than just putting it into
landfill.
But this, I believe, is probably the area where
I think there is the most excitement in terms of driving
real change across Australia and NSW Health, that this is
where we can - this is where innovation is required. We
need partnerships. We need partnerships with other
government agencies, we need partnerships with the private
sector and the university research sector to help us solve
some big challenges. And I think later in my presentation,
I give an example of what we've been trying to do with
gloves that we utilise, but this is an enormous challenge
for us and we need, I think, less bureaucracy and a little
bit of freedom in this particular space to trial and pilot
things. I think that's one of the things that would help
us progress that particular element of waste more rapidly.
Q. If we go back to the slides, please. The second point
on that page:
Reduce our environmental impact while
continuing to focus on Excellence ...
The concept there is --
A. The concept there - yeah, sorry, the concept there
is - sorry, did I cut you off? I apologise.
Q. No, you go. You go?
A. Okay.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Mr Glover can't give the answer as
well as ask the question, so you give the answer and we'll
go from there.
A. This is - I deliberately put this in when we first set
up the program because, having worked in Health, there is
always arguments about where you spend your money, and even
more so now with the tight fiscal environment that we find
ourselves in. This is there to ensure that everyone
remembers that delivering clinical care is our core
business, and --
Q. So whatever you are doing about environmental impact
and reducing emissions, it's not at the expense of

providing good clinical care, right?
A. Perfect.
Q. Yes.
A. And all of the initiatives that we put forward do not
take any money away from frontline clinical services. In
fact, the majority of them return money to those
frontline clinical services. So that's a core fundamental.
It's meant that we've had no opposition. From a change
perspective, no-one has said, "This is a bad idea, because
I can't afford A, B and C in my emergency department." So
strategically, it is a very important position for us to
have. And the third item there is Hunter New England is
the largest employer in this region. We are the largest
LHD in the State and one of the biggest in the country. We
have the opportunity - and I think we've achieved this - to
be real leaders in this particular space and, more
importantly, start to drive a change in our market, the
people we buy stuff from, that they know this is where
we're heading and they start shifting the products they
produce for us so that they become more and more
sustainable.
MR GLOVER: Q. Can we go to the next slide, please.
Could you just take us through?
A. Absolutely. These are the results of our third year
of performance, and we established four high-level KPIs:
CO2 emissions, rainwater captured and reused, water
recycled re-used and waste going to landfill. They are the
four elements we have been focusing on. Along the top
line, you will see our 2020 baseline for each of those
elements; and then, on the bottom line, you'll see our
target for the third year, for 2023; and then in the
circles above, you'll see what we have actually achieved in
2023. So if I just run through each one of those quickly:
CO2, our baseline was 100,000 tonnes. Our target was
30 per cent decrease. We've just met that target at
31 per cent.
In terms of rainwater captured and reused, we were
only doing that in 5 per cent of our facilities in 2020.
We set ourselves a target for 30 per cent in year three and
we are nearly at our fourth-year target. Essentially, we
are looking for a 10 per cent improvement each year on each
of those elements.

Water recycled and re-used. We will always need water
in a health facility. We will always need to wash
something, wash hands or clean something, but we were
looking at a decrease in our water usage and we are just
shy of the target at 28 per cent.
And then the final element, which I mentioned earlier,
is landfill. We wanted a 30 per cent decrease in waste
going to landfill. We didn't achieve that. We are at the
24 per cent metric for this particular year.
Q. Thank you. Go to the next slide, please. These are
recurrent savings achieved in the 2023 period?
A. That's correct, after year three. And just to put
this in context, the most amount of money we've spent has
been in the installation of solar panels across the
district. So the John Hunter solar panel installation,
which I mentioned earlier, cost us about $3.5 million to
$4 million. The balance of all the solar installations we
are putting on solar on every single one of our buildings
across the district, that's about the same money again. So
we've borrowed from Treasury, via a very low interest loan,
about $8 million. We are paying that loan off, and we are
paying that off over the next four to six years, we'll have
it all paid off. So this recurrent savings reflects us
paying off money in parallel. So once we've paid back that
principal, that loan that we've --
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Sorry, how do I understand that?
The 3.38 million in recurrent savings takes into account
your interest payments, or it doesn't?
A. It does.
Q. Yep, great. Okay.
A. So I'll just - John Hunter is a really good example.
So we borrowed the $3.5 million-odd for that. We are
paying back the loan. We are paying that off over six
years and we're paying off - I'm just trying to do the
maths in my head now. My mathematical skills are failing
me.
Q. You can get back to us in relation to any sums rather
than doing them in your head on the run.
A. Thanks, Commissioner. We're paying back about
$500,000 to $600,000 a year in that loan, but we are saving
about $1 million a year in our energy bill at John Hunter
Hospital, so that $400,000 that we --

Q. You're in front.
A. Yes. We're in front, essentially. And that's one
of - and if you were to - a simple decision for government
would be to put solar panels on everything that they own
and they would see a return immediately and set them up for
the future. It is a no-brainer, as far as I'm concerned.
MR GLOVER: Q. Can I just ask you about the three
largest components of this graph. The first being solar,
1.37 million. What is the saving that's under the category
"Solar" in that chart?
A. That's from all the solar panels we've introduced
across the district. And then you'll see electricity; if
you split that out, electricity is really a movement to LED
lighting --
Q. I see.
A. -- across the district and energy reduction
initiatives that we've put in place, sensor lights and the
like.
Q. We'll perhaps come to those in some later slides. And
then the next largest is "Natural Gas"?
A. Yes.
Q. Where are those savings being driven?
A. Yes. So a lot of our - and this is occurring with our
new facilities. A lot of our existing chillers that we use
to air-condition our facilities run off natural gas. We're
moving away from those and utilising electricity now. It
is called "electrification", so John Hunter Hospital will
be the first level 6 trauma hospital in New South Wales
that will be electrified, ie, no gas, no natural gas. So
when we do get green energy, it will all be green and we
won't have to worry about natural gas.
Q. Thank you. Before we leave that slide, these are at
2023. Is it the case that once the initiative is rolled
out across the district, you expect those overall recurrent
savings to continue to rise?
A. Absolutely. I'm hoping that by the time we get to
year 10 and we've paid back those loans, we would be closer
to the $15 million mark. That's just in the areas that
we're focusing on. I'm hoping that if we make some big
breakthroughs in the waste area that that figure could go
up, but it's going to require a few innovative

breakthroughs and some legislative change, I think, to make
this sort of - the waste piece be a bigger component in
terms of savings.
Q. Can we go to the next slide, please. There, six
components of the initiative described. We have heard
about energy, water and waste. Can you just tell us
briefly about "Transport", "Procurement" and
"Infrastructure", please?
A. Absolutely. So transport, our strategies there are
fairly straightforward. One is to move our current
combustible fleet vehicles to electric or electric hybrid.
The reason we've gone - and we've started with hybrid
vehicles. The big drawback to going fully electric has
really been out in regional New South Wales, that to have
the infrastructure to charge the vehicles hasn't existed to
date, but Treasury have recently provided a substantial
amount of money to our district to rollout charging
stations, particularly in our regional areas, so we're in
the process of doing that right now. So it allows more
electric vehicles as we progress.
The other thing we're doing, too, is working with our
clinicians and our staff to think about whether they need
to get in a fleet vehicle and whether they're - we've had
lots of staff saying they'd like to get on an electric
bike, so we've facilitated that. So swapping out fleet
vehicles for electric bikes.
The other few things we've done in transport is
we've - for the first time in the country, we've set up
with the salary packaging groups that all government
agencies engage with to allow our staff to salary sacrifice
to purchase an e-bike, encouraging staff to ride to work
instead of bringing their car, which, of course,
contributes to emissions, but also contributes to the
congestion, particularly at our bigger hospitals. If more
staff could ride, then there is more parking left for
patients and carers.

clinical service. So we have established the physical and

Q. Thank you. I think I interrupted you. You were about
to tell us about other initiatives?
A. Yes. I guess one of the other initiatives that has
recently been established is our bush tucker partnership
with the - where an AMS in Port Macquarie that has been

contribution from our Aboriginal medical service to
establish a program of works that connection our community
with traditional bush tucker food, and using that as a
platform not only to create awareness for the community
around healthy eating choices and lifestyle but also to
connect people in that same fashion around social
prescribing, creating a network, creating a bond over
healthy food and bush tucker, but also then using that to

or prostate.

Q. You don't immediately get, for want of a better

MR FULLER: Q. Can I ask you now, Ms Wong, to put on one
of your other hats, which is in relation to allied health.
You have told us in your statement that you are
strategically, operationally and professionally responsible
for allied health professionals in your district. Can I
just ask you what you mean by "professionally
responsible"?
A. So as the director of allied health, I have a
professional responsibility to all allied health
professionals in the Mid North Coast Local Health District.
I do not have operational management of all allied health
staff in the district. So from a professional perspective,
I am responsible for all 17 of the professions that are
represented out of the 23 that are recognised, and I am
responsible for providing that strategic and professional
leadership and advocacy on behalf of allied health.
Q. Can I ask you, please, to have a look at paragraph 35
of your statement. This is there paragraph where you made
some changes to earlier. I am just going to ask you, about
halfway down the paragraph, you talk about a 3.3 per cent
growth rate in allied health for your district compared
with an average of 12.6 per cent across rural or regional
LHDs and 9.1 per cent across the State. Do you have any
sense from your position as to why the growth rate in

allied health is so much lower in your district than in
others?
A. There's a range of factors that I believe contribute
to that. Some of that is around workforce pipeline and the
ability to attract staff to our area. I do believe that
some of that is also around the type of - the funding that
is available for allied health and also the workforce that
is available in regards to the positions. Some allied
health positions are multidisciplinary classed, which means
that they can be an allied health profession or a nursing
profession, and so depending on the successful applicant,
we might have seen a growth in nursing for that particular
position as opposed to allied health, but in natural
attrition the next person who might fill that position may
be allied health. Ability to attract skilled workforce to
the Mid North Coast Local Health District across allied
health professions is very challenging.
Q. You have told us in your statement that the retention
rate for allied health professionals in your district is,
I think it is fair to say, relatively high, greater than
90 per cent. Is that a fair observation?
A. That is a fair observation.

A. Yes. So I would say that the main issue was
attraction to new funding or funding opportunities, as well

factor in for temporary vacancies, so parental leave,
maternity leave, or other secondments, and that temporary
aspect of vacancy again is very challenging to fill or to
attract people from out of area to move into the Mid North
Coast for a time-limited period.
Q. So even though you might have a high retention rate on
paper, you do still have vacancies as a result of things
like parental leave that you find difficult to fill?
A. To fill, yes.
Q. Just starting with "pipeline", which is one of the
causes that you mentioned, you have told us in paragraph 40
about junior practitioners who say there is an opportunity

NSW Health. Can I just ask you to elaborate on what you
mean by that?
A. So my comment around - sorry, excuse me.

Q. It's about halfway down paragraph 40.
A. The "better prepare practitioners in relation to the
specific requirements for NSW Health"?
Q. Yes?
A. So what we have been seeing in the Mid North Coast is
new graduates choosing to work as private practitioners in
the area. If a new graduate graduates and applies for a
role with NSW Health, they will often be remunerated at a
level 1 year 4 rate, and within our award that equates to
roughly $38 to $40 an hour. Those new graduates can work
in the private market with an MBS rate of approximately $75
for an intervention, and if we consider that from just a
numerical perspective, it is very lucrative for new
graduates to work in that space, or any allied health
professional.
What we do hear and see is that working in private
practice as a sole practitioner in a small practice does
not have the same framework that you would have in a Mid
North Coast Local Health District or NSW Health frame,
where there is the embedding of clinical supervision, the
support of clinical mentoring, professional growth and
development, but also that framework and structure of
exposure and support to clinical practice and development.
We use a notional post, years post-qualification, to
assist us in benchmarking a qualified professional against
the current allied health award, and after a couple of
years, you know, I have written two to four years of
post-graduate experience in a private practice, those staff
may be eligible to apply for a more senior allied health
role, however, have not had the benefit of understanding
some of the supporting structures that exist within the
allied health professional workforce such as the mentoring,
the clinical supervision, the research aspects to clinical
care and the, you know, policy and procedures and design
that goes alongside clinical care.
Q. Just to understand the two to four years, is that - is
the idea there that after they have spent two to - sorry.
The amount that they are paid in private practice is
equivalent to something like two to four years
post-graduate under the relevant award, if they were to
work in the NSW Health system?
A. Yes, it is much closer in an hourly rate estimate.

Q. And that would be why more junior people would tend to
be attracted to more senior positions in the NSW Health
system compared with private practice; is that the idea?
A. That is my understanding and what we are experiencing
anecdotally.
Q. And the other part of your answer is the general idea
that in a world where a new graduate will be paid so much
less in the NSW Health system compared with private
practice, there need to be other reasons that make it
attractive for them to come and work in the NSW Health
system?
A. Yes.
Q. Is that - that's the idea?
A. That's the idea. I think that's also coupled with,
perhaps, some missed opportunity to support student
placements within the local health district. So there are
two factors that we are experiencing around the challenge
to attract students to undertake student placements to give
experience or insight into what it's like to work within
the LHD system, and then also the remuneration variation.
Q. Sorry, you mentioned two factors. Can you just
clarify what are the two factors?
A. Student placements. So having students experience
their time within the LHD system as an addition to why
people might choose to work in private practice, being the
remuneration aspect.
Q. You have told us - or just starting with student
placements, can you just tell us firstly what you perceive
the issue to be there?
A. Yes. For me, I perceive the issue is that there's no
set way to facilitate student placements for our allied
health professional groups. This is often undertaken on a
local basis with the relevant tertiary institutes. It's
not a consistent, I guess, pathway for all students. Some
professional groups require one-day-a-week-type models for
student placements, others replace block placements at
different times of the year. We also have a competitive
market with private practice. So we are aware in Mid North
Coast that some private practices offer student placements
as well as a part-time job or a temporary role which

clinical placement. Those, I guess, flexibilities or

nuances are not necessarily available within the Mid North
Coast Local Health District structure.

structure.

address those issues?

is the diversity for allied health as a professional, you
know, cohort of 23. I think that there are opportunities
to strengthen our allied health clinical educators embedded
within our local health district. There would be
opportunities to look at how we partner with our tertiary
facilities - sorry, tertiary institutes on how we utilise
our maximise student placements, how many students are
coming through our public health system, and at what times
and rates. We could be looking or exploring opportunities
to subsidise the cost of accommodation for those students
who need to travel from out-of-area to be placed in a rural
setting. We could enhance or prioritise, perhaps, rural
LHDs or rural settings for clinical placements for allied
health professionals and students going through their
education.

Queensland, there is a different award structure for their
allied health professionals where there are some incentives
for the employed allied health professionals within the
Queensland system to support and mentor students, but
there's also some more formalised agreements with the
universities to support placements within the state system.

perhaps we could consider looking at and to see the
feasibility within NSW Health.

Queensland there are some incentives for employed allied
health professionals to support and mentor students, do you
have any sense of what is the nature of those incentives?

have an allied health award, they have an enterprise
bargaining agreement and they provide, I guess, additional
incentive payments or - I'm not sure what you would call

it. Like, a payment on top of their hourly rate to
undertake higher study or education relating to their role,
but also then to provide that clinical mentorship to a
student or a junior allied health professional.
Q. So it might be like a clinical educator allowance --
A. Yes.
Q. -- if someone is prepared to perform that role?
A. Yes.

allied health clinical educators, can you just explain what

workforce that related to allied health clinical educators
that showed that across the State, on average, there is one
allied health clinical educator for every 420 full-time
equivalent. In contrast, if I can use nursing as an

educator or clinical midwifery educator for every 42,
I think, FTE. And I am aware that I've - 43, apologies.
43 FTE.

At the moment, Mid North Coast has one allied health
clinical educator with a radiography background, but given
the diversity of the allied health professional workforce

that workforce pipeline through clinical education not only
provides career opportunities for our current workforce,
but it also helps to stabilise or to create that pipeline
in the coming years. It then takes away the pressure on an
individual LHD or somebody, I suppose, in my role, to make
a decision around value for whether we pause or reduce some
of the clinical services that we're providing to re-divert
some of that into clinical education, which may not be
patient-facing work, but is still extraordinarily important
in regards to the whole system of workforce sustainability.
Q. Can you just explain for us practically what the
allied health clinical educator in your district does?

What is their job?

responsibility is specific to the radiography profession
and cohort, and their role would be not only to facilitate
the student placements coming through, but to provide an
upskill on education best practice literature and ensuring
that all of the staff within that cohort are up-to-date
within their practice.

universities to maximise clinical placements. Do you have
any views on how that might be done practically?

to navigate what that placement might look like. For
allied health, we are very unique because there is such
diversity but allied health professionals within a
university structure are not within the same school of
education either. So we're not negotiating with one school
within a university; we have to navigate and negotiate, and
partner, with a range of different clinical schools. So
the, I guess, logistics of planning for placements is
challenging.

success, it's outside of allied health but there has been
establishment of the rural medical clinical schools in both
Port Macquarie and in Macksville/Coffs Harbour, and those
schools have been really successful to date around taking a
more tailored approach to supporting students who are
undertaking their studies in this geographical area, but
also supporting them with placements in our LHD.
So spreading out those placements to be, you know, for
example, one day a week so there is some continuity, broken
up with their tutorials and clinic days across the week, so
there is a sustainability visibility for those students to
also have part-time work and then they're living and
working within the regional setting of the Mid North Coast,
greater supports around social networks and stability
around accommodation and housing because they're here for a
longer period of time, and, hopefully, we will continue to
see the retention of those students once they graduate in
wanting to stay and work within Mid North Coast Local
Health District.
Q. Am I right in understanding that for allied health,
your district does not have a clinical placement

coordinator or facilitator?
A. That's correct.
Q. Do you think that would help in addressing some of the
logistical issues that you have identified?
A. Absolutely.

midwifery where there is dedicated clinical placement
coordinator position; have I understood that correctly?
A. That is correct.

subsidised accommodation. Can you just explain why is
accommodation cost an issue for students in your district?
A. I've drawn a conclusion that when we are having
difficulties attracting staff or workforce to vacant
positions because of an inability to access affordable
accommodation that that would absolutely be a factor for
students who are not necessarily earning money while they
are undertaking their clinical placement. So without
having access to a level of subsidised accommodation or
without students actually residing in the area already,
there is, I guess, a barrier in place for those students
being able to travel to the Mid North Coast to undertake
that placement.

statement, which deals with opportunities for innovation
and reform. Firstly, in paragraph 53, you say that, in the
first sentence, there is an appetite from the community and
clinicians for the provision of clinical care virtually and
to embed this as part of our normal practice. When you say
there is an "appetite", what is your reason for thinking
that?

high uptake and the positive experiences based on the
patients that we have provided care to through Mid North
Coast Virtual Care and some of our other virtual care
services such as Enhancing Community Care. I think
stereotypically or anecdotally, we would have thought
perhaps there would have been a lower uptake. There is
commentary around concerns raised anecdotally around our
aged population being comfortable using a device to access
care when we historically have always undertaken to access
care face-to-face and in person.

Mid North Coast has a significant - a proportion of
our population over the age of 65, but the utilisation
rates and the positive experience reports and the positive
outcome measures that we have been collecting show that
there is appetite from the community that they are willing
to, and want to, use virtual care where it's appropriate,
and I think that we can embed this more broadly as part of
the way we deliver care.
I think that there will always be a place for
face-to-face care; of course we need to have that as
modality, but there are aspects of care that can be
provided through telehealth or audiovisual means.
Q. Part of what you suggest should be done to try to
embed virtual care as part of normal practice is to shift
community expectations around the provision of remote care.
Do you have anything in particular in mind as to how that
might be done in practice?
A. I think we've been lucky in the Mid North Coast that
we had some very good success with COVID. We used virtual
care and telehealth to provide what we then called COVID
care in the community, to keep our community safe and well
at home. We had a very low admission rate in that COVID
pandemic era. I guess the community expectations, because
of that experience, was somewhat forced. People had to use
technology to remain connected. That community expectation
shifting and, I guess, marketing of how we can deliver very
sound, safe, effective and efficient care through a virtual
platform, is an opportunity to continue shifting or
supporting that community expectation.

on positive experiences is assisting in shifting community
expectations where we often have community members using
our services, asking our permission to post on social media
their experience with us, or on the various, you know,
groups within social media for the townships that we have,
to share their positive experience, and I think that
creates awareness in the community around being able to
access care in a way that's different to how we have
historically.

from community clinicians for the provision of clinical

about virtual care services and, in particular, the Mid

Q. In paragraph 57, you have told us that there are
opportunities to shift the focus and understanding on the
value of multidisciplinary clinical care models and
structures within NSW Health systems. Can I ask you,
please, just to explain what you mean by that?
A. This comment, and what I mean by this is around
multidisciplinary care being care provided by allied health
professionals as well as nurses and doctors. And, I guess,
when I talk about marketing and celebrating the value
proposition, I think at the moment we still see or we still
have a general vision of health being provided primarily by
doctors and nurses. It's in the media that we see. It's
on television shows that are free-to-air. It is the
general understanding of the community. More rarely do we
see the value celebrated of an allied health professional
workforce in care in contemporary media, and I think that
there is an opportunity for us to share and celebrate, but
also provide awareness on the value that that
multidisciplinary or holistic clinical care team can
provide.
Q. You said that reliance or emphasis on high cost
medical models in nursing has a direct impact on allied
health resourcing, but also the ability to fulfil best
patient care. Can you explain why you think that has an
impact on patient care?
A. So my understanding of how we can best deliver patient
care is to take a holistic approach in how we provide
person-centred care using a multidisciplinary care team, so
allied health, nursing and medical. Unfortunately, we have
varying models and frames that sit around our different
clinical groups. So nurses have a nursing hours per
patient day ratio that is written into our systems and
awards, and that is a requirement for us as a local health
district to meet and fulfil, and that is to ensure that
there is a safe ratio of nurses to patients in the acute
setting.

equivalent version. There's not a set allied health hours
per patient day and nor is there a set statewide metric
around workload management for allied health, and as such,
when we are needing to make decisions in a fiscally
constrained environment, we need to ensure that we are
fulfilling all of the requirements of our clinical team and
then looking at how we can invest and reallocate within the
envelope of funding that we have. And that goes to my

comment around at times this has a direct impact to allied
health resourcing because there is not the equivalent of,
you know, a metric such as nursing hours per patient day,
which sometimes mean we have to make a very challenging
decision around where to use a very limited pool of
funding.
Q. The other point concerning that sentence is, or the
other impact you mention in that sentence, is on the whole
cycle of workforce sustainability. Can you just elaborate
on what you mean by that, please?

have a large vacancy across that nursing pool. Limited
supply for the high demand means reliance on locum or
agency nurses, which come at a premium cost, and that cost

sustainability. So if we are relying on paying for premium
labour across medical or nursing or allied health, because

the baseline of our workforce across all of the different
professionals groups, we are then needing to expend more
than expected to fill that baseline.

patient care, then over time we would expect to reduce the
burden on nurses and therefore the need to rely on, for

workforce?

grow our diversity in our clinical workforce, the less we
are reliant on one particular supply and demand chain. So
not necessarily taking away from the value of nurses or the
need for nurses, but if we had more allied health as well
as nurses as well as medical, we would be less impacted by
the reliance on one singular supply and demand chain.

saying in paragraph 59, "opportunities to consider the
reporting obligations, and return on investment
considerations", I understand, at least I think, part of

extended but it might not, and then if it's not extended,
difficult decisions have to be made. That's part of what
you are getting at there, is it?

investment is of some of these programs that are only

done as to whether they should be extended?

Q. Is there any particular example you would like to draw
my attention to to make good that, or is it a general
observation?

Sexual Abuse, we had a range of recommendations and
